facts.claim: Google’s SRE Workbook defines canarying as a partial and time-limited deployment of a change, and its evaluation: the part that gets the change is the canary, the rest is the control.
The same chapter calls canarying effectively an A/B test: if the canary’s error ratio is similar to the control’s, the deployment goes on.
It warns that a check that is overly strict gives lots of false positives, and that a canary should last long enough to be representative.
For a bad canary, it says to pause and roll back the deployment, or call a person to help.
Pete Hodgson, on martinfowler.com, describes feature toggles as patterns for delivering new functionality rapidly but safely, separating a feature’s release from the code’s deployment.
Danilo Sato (martinfowler.com, 2014) describes parallel change for backward-incompatible changes: expand to support old and new, migrate every user, then contract to remove the old.
DORA measures software delivery with change lead time, deployment frequency, change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time and deployment rework rate.
DORA defines failed deployment recovery time as the time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and needs immediate intervention.
